sentences.text: The accused persons in S.T. No. 2161 of 2007 on the files of the Court of the Judicial Magistrate of First Class-I, Kochi, are the revision petitioners.

entities.text: Judicial Magistrate of First Class-I, Kochi
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: The first revision petitioner was convicted and sentenced under Section 16 (1)(a)(i) read with Section 2 (ia)(j) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (hereinafter called as "the PFA Act") and the second revision petitioner was convicted and sentenced under Sections 16 (1)(a)(i) and 2 (ia)(j) of PFA Act and Rule 50 (1) of Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules (hereinafter called as "the PFA Rules) read with Section 16 (1)(a)(ii) of the PFA Act.

2. Heard both sides.
3.

The prosecution allegation is that on 13-6-2007 at about 1 p.m., PW1, the Food Inspector purchased 9 Crl.R.P. No. 492 of 2014 2 :-
pieces of fried chicken from the first accused.
The second accused was the licensee of the said shop.
After sampling as per Rules, one sample was sent to the Public Analyst for analysis.
The Public Analyst submitted Ext. P12 report stating that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for the food item.
It was also reported that the sample contained added synthetic food colour sunset yellow FCF in contravention of Rule 29 of the PFA Rules, 1955 and was, therefore adulterated.
4 . Before the trial Court, PW1 to PW12 were examined and Exts. P1 to P21 were marked for the prosecution.
Ext. X1 was also marked.
DW1 was examined for the revision petitioners.

5. The learned counsel for the revision petitioners has submitted that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext. P12 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated.

The learned counsel for Crl.R.P. No.
492 of 2014 3 :-
the revision petitioner relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument.

entities.text: Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
6. In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was prescribed as mandated under Section 23 (1-A)

2 (ee) and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act.

entities.text: Ayush vs The State Of Kerala
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Therefore, Ext. P12 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra).

It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal.

In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court Crl.R.P. No.
492 of 2014 4 :-
acquitted the accused.
The matter was referred to a Division Bench and the Division Bench also affirmed the said decision, submitted by the learned counsel for the petitioner and the learned Public Prosecutor.

Even otherwise, in view of the direction in Pepsico (Supra), the conviction in this case under Section 16 (1)(a)(i) read with Section 2 (ia)(j) of the PFA Act cannot be sustained and consequently, the conviction and sentence passed by the courts below against the revision petitioners under Sections 16(1)(a)(i) and 2 (ia)(j) of the PFA Act, stand set aside and the revision petitioners are acquitted for the said offence.
7. The courts below concurrently found that the second revision petitioner sold the food article without having any valid licence under the PFA Rules during the relevant period.
There is no material before the Court to show that the second revision petitioner had any valid licence to sell the food item during the relevant period.
The incident in this case was on 13-6-2007.
There is no previous conviction against the 2nd revision petitioner.

Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, I am Crl.R.P. No. 492 of 2014 5 :-
of the view that the 2nd revision petitioner can be sentenced as provided under the 2nd proviso to Section 16 (1) of the PFA Act and

accordingly, the sentence awarded by the courts below against the second revision petitioner stands modified and reduced to imprisonment till the rising of the court and a fine of Rs. 500/- (Rupees five hundred only) and in default to simple imprisonment for 5 days under Section 16 (1)(a) (ii) of the PFA Act read with Rule 50 (1) of the PFA Rules, to meet the ends of justice.
In the result, this Revision Petition stands allowed in part as above.
The 2nd revision petitioner shall surrender before the trial court on 20-5-2016 to suffer the sentence.
B. SUDHEENDRA KUMAR, JUDGE.
